karten: What are the 4 basic bookings (4 cards)?
1 Purchase: stock + input VAT to payables. 2 Sale: receivables to revenue + output VAT. 3 Stock adjustment: VAK to stock. 4 Payment: payables to bank or bank to receivables.
What does VAK mean and when is it booked?
„Verrechnete Anschaffungskosten“ = cost of goods sold at cost price. With every sale: VAK to stock (expense booking).
How do you book payment of an incoming invoice with cash discount?
Payables (full amount) to bank (amount paid), net cash discount (cash discount income or stock account) and input VAT correction.
How do you book a customer payment with cash discount?
Bank (amount paid), net cash discount (cash discount expense or revenue account) and output VAT correction to receivables (full amount).
What is margin taxation (§ 25a UStG, „Differenzbesteuerung“)?

VAT is only due on the difference between selling and purchase price. Requirement: purchase without input VAT deduction (e.g. from a private seller). VAT = difference × 19/119. No VAT shown on the invoice.
How is a margin-taxed used car sale booked?

1400 receivables to 8110 Revenue used cars (margin taxed) (purchase price), 8111 extra revenue (net margin), 1770 VAT (from the margin). Then 7110 VAK used cars (margin taxed) to 3110 Used car stock (margin taxed).
What is the old-part tax („Altteilsteuer“)?
For exchange parts, the old part counts as part of the payment: 10 % of the exchange part price × 19 % is added to the normal VAT (account 1795).
How do you work back from the amount transferred after cash discount to the invoice amount?

The customer has already deducted the discount. So the amount transferred is not 100 % but, for example, 98 % of the invoice (with 2 % discount). That is why you must not simply add 2 %; you work back from the reduced value to 100 %. Formula to remember: invoice amount = amount paid / (1 − discount rate), e.g. ÷ 0,98.
How do you get from gross to net and to the VAT included?

The gross amount already contains the VAT: gross is 119 %, net is 100 %. So you do not subtract 19 % of the gross amount; you divide by 1,19. The VAT included is the difference between gross and net. Formula to remember: net = gross / 1,19; VAT = gross × 19 / 119.
Name the steps of trade pricing.

List purchase price − discount = purchase price on credit − cash discount = cash purchase price + delivery costs = landed cost + overheads = cost price + profit = cash selling price + customer cash discount = selling price on credit + customer discount = net list selling price + VAT = gross selling price.
Explain when forward, backward or difference pricing is used.
Forward: selling price wanted. Backward: selling price given, highest purchase price wanted. Difference: both prices fixed, profit wanted.
Explain what the markup, the pricing factor and the trade margin tell you.

All three describe the gap between purchase price and selling price, just from different angles. The markup says what percentage is added to the landed cost. The pricing factor sums this up in one number to multiply by. The trade margin says what percentage of the selling price remains for the dealer to cover costs and make a profit. Formula to remember: markup = (net SP − landed cost) / landed cost × 100; factor = net SP / landed cost; margin = (net SP − landed cost) / net SP × 100.
Explain why customer cash discount and customer discount are calculated „im Hundert“ (on the higher base).
Because the customer deducts them from the higher price. The cash selling price is e.g. 98 % of the selling price on credit, so divide by 0,98.
Name the three stages of cost accounting (KLR).
Cost type accounting (which costs?), cost centre accounting (where? overhead sheet BAB), cost unit accounting (for what? pricing).
Distinguish between expense and cost.
Expense: total consumption of value per P&L. Cost: only the operational, period-appropriate, ordinary consumption of value.
Explain the term neutral expenses and give examples.
Expenses that are not costs: non-operational (donation), relating to other periods (tax back payment), extraordinary (fire damage).
Explain basic costs, different costs and additional costs, each with an example.

Basic costs: expense = cost. Different costs: expense in a different amount (imputed depreciation, imputed risks, imputed interest instead of interest paid on debt). Additional costs: no expense (imputed entrepreneur's salary, imputed rent, imputed interest on equity).
Explain why an imputed entrepreneur's salary is charged.
In an e. K., OHG or KG the owner receives no salary. So that his work goes into prices and comparison with a GmbH/AG is fair, a salary is set.
Distinguish between direct costs and overheads and give one example of each from a dealership.
Direct costs can be assigned directly: cost price of vehicle/part, productive wages, commission. Overheads only via an allocation key: rent, admin salaries, energy, advertising.
Name the tasks of the overhead sheet (BAB).
Distribute overheads to cost centres, allocate service cost centres to main cost centres, determine overhead rates, control costs.
Name the four main cost centres of a dealership.
New cars, used cars, parts and accessories, workshop (customer service). Administration is a service cost centre.
Distinguish between main and service cost centres.
Main cost centres provide services for the market and charge their costs to cost units. Service cost centres work for other centres and are allocated to them.
Explain the overhead rate and what it is used for.

Overheads such as rent or administration cannot be assigned directly to a job. The overhead rate still spreads them as fairly as possible: it says what percentage of overheads is added to the direct costs of a cost centre. That way every job can be costed with its full costs. In the workshop the base is productive wages, in trade it is the cost of goods sold (VAK). Formula to remember: overheads of the cost centre / direct costs of the cost centre × 100.
Name suitable allocation keys for rent, energy, depreciation and advertising.
Rent: floor space. Energy: consumption. Depreciation: asset values. Advertising: revenue. Phone: lines. Entrepreneur's salary: time shares.
Distinguish between full cost and partial cost accounting.
Full cost: all costs to cost units, for long-term prices. Partial cost: only variable costs, fixed costs as a block, for short-term decisions.
Explain the term contribution margin.
Revenue − variable costs. The amount that contributes to covering fixed costs and then to profit.
Name two examples each of variable and fixed costs in a dealership.
Variable: cost of goods, salesperson commission, productive wages. Fixed: rent, admin salaries, depreciation, insurance.
Explain the short-term and the long-term price floor.
Short-term: variable unit costs (CM = 0). Long-term: full cost per unit (all costs covered).
Describe the structure of multi-level contribution margin accounting (KER).
Revenue − variable costs I = CM 1 (gross profit) − variable costs II (sales-related) = CM 2 − division fixed costs = CM 3 − company fixed costs = operating result.
Explain the break-even point.

The sales volume at which revenue exactly covers total costs: no profit, no loss. Every unit sold brings a contribution margin (price minus variable costs), which first pays off the fixed costs. Once the fixed costs are covered, every further unit brings profit. Formula to remember: break-even quantity = fixed costs / contribution margin per unit.
Explain the hourly labour rate.
Price of one workshop hour for the customer. Covers wages, all workshop overheads, risk and profit.
Explain the workshop index.

It shows what multiple of productive wages the workshop must charge its customers so that wages, overheads, risk and profit are covered. Example: an index of 3,8 means 3,80 € must be earned for every 1 € of mechanic's wages. The higher the index, the higher the overheads in relation to wages. The profit and risk mark-ups are both calculated on cost. Formula to remember: target labour revenue / productive wages (or hourly rate / average wage).
Describe how to determine the hourly rate from an invoice with labour units (AW).

Labour units are the manufacturer's time units. The invoice shows the labour charge for a certain number of AW. Dividing the charge by the AW gives the price per AW. Because several AW make one hour, you scale this price up to one hour. Formula to remember: net labour price / AW charged × AW per hour (e.g. 10 or 100 AW per hour).
Distinguish between productive and unproductive wages.
Productive: mechanic hours chargeable directly to customer orders. Unproductive: not chargeable, e.g. tidying, training, waiting time, workshop master, stores.
Explain why the warranty hourly rate is lower.
The manufacturer sets the payment rate and labour times. The business cannot calculate it freely.
Explain what the equity ratio tells you.

It shows what share of total capital belongs to the company itself. The higher it is, the more independent the company is of banks and suppliers, the better it can absorb losses and the more creditworthy it is. Formula to remember: equity / total capital × 100.
Explain what liquidity levels 1, 2 and 3 tell you.

They show whether the company can pay its short-term debts, using more and more assets: level 1 only with cash (cash in hand, bank), level 2 also with receivables, level 3 with all current assets. Rule of thumb: level 2 should be at least 100 %, level 3 clearly more. Formula to remember: the respective assets / short-term debt × 100.
Explain what return on equity, on total capital and on sales tell you.

Return means: how well does the money invested pay off? Return on equity shows the interest earned on the owners' money, to compare with a safe investment. Return on total capital shows the interest earned on all capital, which is why interest on debt counts towards the result. Return on sales shows how many cents of profit remain from each euro of revenue. Formula to remember: profit / equity; (profit + interest on debt) / total capital; profit / revenue; each × 100.
Explain what return on sales tells you.
What percentage of revenue remains as profit, i.e. how many cents of profit per euro of revenue.
Explain the golden balance sheet rule.
Long-term assets should be financed long term. Strict: equity covers fixed assets. Less strict: equity + long-term debt cover them.
Explain the leverage effect.
If the return on total capital is above the interest rate on debt, additional debt increases the return on equity.
Explain the operating result, the neutral result and the company result.
Operating result = output − costs. Neutral result = neutral income − neutral expenses. Together: company result (P&L).
Explain what the stock ratios tell you.

Average stock shows how much capital is tied up in the warehouse. The turnover rate says how often the stock is sold and replenished in a year. The storage period says how many days goods stay in stock on average. The aim is a high turnover and a short storage period, because this saves interest, space and risk (obsolescence, shrinkage). Formula to remember: Ø stock = (opening + closing stock) / 2; turnover rate = cost of goods / Ø stock; storage period = 360 / turnover rate.
Distinguish between horizontal and vertical balance sheet analysis.
Vertical: structure of one side (e.g. equity ratio, fixed asset intensity). Horizontal: assets to liabilities (fixed asset coverage, liquidity).
Name the components of the acquisition cost.
Net purchase price − price reductions (discount, cash discount) + incidental acquisition costs (freight, installation, registration).
Explain straight-line depreciation.

A fixed asset loses value through use. With straight-line depreciation this loss is spread evenly over the useful life: the same amount every year. In the year of purchase it is depreciated pro rata by month, starting with the month of purchase. Formula to remember: amount = acquisition cost / useful life; rate = 100 / useful life.
Explain the term low-value asset (GWG).
„Geringwertiges Wirtschaftsgut“: movable, wears out, usable on its own, up to 800 € net. May be written off in full immediately.
Name possible causes of a stocktaking difference.
Theft, shrinkage, breakage, counting errors, booking errors, unrecorded withdrawals.
Describe how to calculate the net staffing requirement.
Target headcount − (current headcount + confirmed arrivals − confirmed departures).
Distinguish between replacement, new and reduced staffing requirements.
Replacement: replace leaving employees. New/additional: extra positions. Reduced: positions are cut.
Distinguish between a job description and a job posting.

Job description: internal document that describes a position permanently, regardless of who holds it: title, position in the hierarchy (superiors, subordinates, deputy), goals, tasks, authority, responsibility, requirements. Job posting: advertisement used to find applicants for a vacant position, internally or externally: company profile, tasks, requirement profile, offer (salary, benefits), start date, how to apply. Memory aid: the description describes the position, the posting looks for someone to fill it.
State the statutory notice periods under § 622 BGB.
Basic period 4 weeks to the 15th or end of month. Probation 2 weeks. Employer: from 2 years 1 month, 5 → 2, 8 → 3, 10 → 4, 12 → 5, 15 → 6, 20 → 7 months to the end of the month.
Describe what applies to fixed-term contracts without objective reason.
At most 2 years, with at most 3 extensions within that, in writing before work starts (TzBfG).
Name the employment papers a leaving employee receives.
Job reference, income tax certificate, holiday certificate, employment certificate for the employment agency, social security notification.
State the statutory minimum leave and the qualifying period.
24 working days with a 6-day week (= 20 days with 5 days). Full entitlement after 6 months, before that 1/12 per full month.
Distinguish between a home office and mobile working.
Home office: permanently set up workplace at home. Mobile working: work from any location.
Describe the levels of legal capacity to contract.
0–6 no capacity. 7–17 limited capacity. From 18 full capacity.
What does the pocket money rule (§ 110 BGB) say?
A person with limited capacity concludes a valid contract if they pay with funds given to them for free use.
Explain the term legal capacity.
Ability to have rights and obligations. Natural persons from birth, legal persons from registration.
Name reasons why a legal transaction is void.
Incapacity, lack of form, violation of law, immorality, sham and joke transactions. Invalid from the start.
Name the reasons why a legal transaction can be contested.
Mistake, fraudulent deception, unlawful threat. Valid until contested.
Distinguish between possession and ownership.
Possession: actual control over the item. Ownership: legal control.
How does ownership of a movable item pass?
By agreement and handover. Payment alone is not enough.
What applies to general terms and conditions (AGB)?
Pre-formulated terms that save negotiation effort. Must be incorporated. Individual agreements take precedence. Invalid clauses drop out, the contract remains.
Describe the buyer's rights in case of a material defect.
First supplementary performance (repair or replacement). Then withdrawal, price reduction, damages. Limitation 2 years.
Explain the reversal of the burden of proof in consumer sales.
If the defect appears in the first 12 months, it is presumed to have existed at handover (§ 477 BGB).
May liability for defects be shortened for consumers?

For new items not below 2 years. For used items to at least 1 year, but only if the consumer was specifically informed before the contract and the shortening is agreed expressly and separately (§ 476 (2) BGB). A clause in the terms and conditions alone is not enough.
Explain the duty to inspect and notify in a commercial sale between merchants.
Inspect goods without delay and report defects without delay. Hidden defects without delay after discovery, within the limitation period.
When is a buyer in default of payment?

With a fixed calendar date when it passes, otherwise by reminder, at the latest 30 days after due date and receipt of invoice. For consumers the 30-day rule only applies if the invoice points it out (§ 286 BGB).
Explain the transfer of ownership by way of security.
The bank becomes owner, the borrower remains possessor and continues to use the item.
Describe the liability and minimum capital of a GmbH.
Only the company's assets are liable. Share capital at least 25.000 €.
Describe the statutory profit distribution in a GmbH.
In proportion to the shares held.
Describe the liability of the partners in an OHG.
All partners have unlimited liability (including private assets), directly and jointly.
What may a „Prokurist“ (holder of general commercial power of attorney) not do?
Sell or encumber land (without special authority), sign the balance sheet, grant „Prokura“, admit partners, sell the company, file for insolvency.
What may a holder of „Handlungsvollmacht“ not do without special authority?
Take out loans, conduct lawsuits, sell or encumber land, enter into bill of exchange liabilities.
Distinguish between sole, joint and branch „Prokura“.
Sole: may represent alone. Joint: only together with another authorised person. Branch: limited to one branch.
Which law governs dual vocational training?
The Vocational Training Act (BBiG).
Explain how an apprenticeship can be terminated after the probationary period.
Apprentice: 4 weeks' notice when giving up or changing occupation. Both: without notice for good cause. In writing with reasons.
State the rules on breaks and working hours under the Youth Employment Protection Act.
Max. 8 hours a day, 40 a week, 5-day week. 30 min break for more than 4,5 to 6 hours, 60 min for more than 6 hours.
Describe the works council election: when it takes place, who may vote and who can be elected.
Every 4 years from 1 March to 31 May. Voting from age 16. Eligible from 18 after 6 months of employment.
Describe the election and voting rights of the youth and apprentice representation (JAV).
Every 2 years from 1 October to 30 November. Voters: under 18 and all apprentices. Eligible: under 25 and apprentices.
Describe the sequence of a collective bargaining dispute.
Termination and negotiation, failure, arbitration, failure, strike ballot, strike, new negotiation, ballot on the result, new collective agreement.
What does the peace obligation mean?
During the term of the collective agreement, industrial action over its content is not allowed.
Who monitors occupational safety?
State trade supervisory authority and employers' liability insurance associations (Berufsgenossenschaften).
How long is sick pay continued?
6 weeks by the employer, then sickness benefit from the health insurance fund.
Name the five branches of social insurance and their providers.
Health (health insurance funds), long-term care (care funds), pension (Deutsche Rentenversicherung), unemployment (Federal Employment Agency), accident (Berufsgenossenschaften).
Who pays accident insurance and what does it cover?
Only the employer. Accidents at work, commuting accidents, occupational diseases.
What does the contribution assessment ceiling mean?
Contributions are calculated up to this gross pay. The part above it remains contribution-free.
Distinguish between income-related expenses and special expenses.
Income-related expenses: costs for the job (travel, work equipment, training). Special expenses: provision expenses, church tax, donations.
Name the conditions of a perfect market.
Homogeneous goods, no preferences (factual, personal, spatial, temporal), full transparency, immediate reaction, many suppliers and buyers.
Explain the functions of the equilibrium price.
Balancing (market clearing), signalling (scarcity), steering (factors of production), selection (inefficient suppliers).
Explain excess supply and a buyer's market.
Price above equilibrium: supply greater than demand. Buyers are in the stronger position, prices come under pressure.
Explain excess demand and a seller's market.
Price below equilibrium: demand greater than supply. Sellers are in the stronger position.
What happens when demand rises (curve shifts right)?
Equilibrium price and quantity rise.
What happens when supply rises (curve shifts right)?
The equilibrium price falls, the quantity rises.
Explain consumer surplus and producer surplus.
Consumer surplus: benefit for buyers who would have paid more. Producer surplus: benefit for suppliers who would have sold for less.
Distinguish between polypoly, supply oligopoly and supply monopoly.
Many suppliers and many buyers. Few suppliers and many buyers. One supplier and many buyers.
Describe the effects of maximum and minimum prices.
Maximum price (below equilibrium): excess demand, black market. Minimum price (above equilibrium): excess supply, the state must buy up surpluses.
Distinguish between market-conforming and market-contrary state interventions.
Market-conforming: price formation stays free (subsidies, taxes, transfers). Market-contrary: price is prescribed (maximum, minimum, fixed price).
Name the actors in the extended economic cycle.
Private households, companies, state, banks (capital collection points), foreign countries.
Distinguish between the maximum and the minimum principle.
Maximum: greatest success with given means. Minimum: a given goal with the least use of means.
Name features of the social market economy.
Private property with social obligation, free price formation, protection of competition, freedom of contract and trade, free collective bargaining, social security and redistribution.
Distinguish between cooperation and concentration of companies.
Cooperation: legally independent companies work together in some areas. Concentration: economic independence is lost (group, merger).
Distinguish between horizontal, vertical and diagonal mergers.
Horizontal: same production/trade level. Vertical: upstream and downstream levels. Diagonal: different industries.
Name the tasks of the Federal Cartel Office.
Enforce the cartel ban, pursue abuse of dominant market positions, control mergers.
Name the goals of the magic square.
Price stability, high employment, external economic balance, steady and appropriate economic growth (Stability Act 1967).
Name a measure for each goal of the magic square.
Inflation rate (consumer price index), unemployment rate, net exports, growth of real GDP.
What is GDP and how is it calculated by expenditure?
Value of all goods and services produced in the country in a year. Private consumption + government consumption + gross investment + (exports − imports).
Distinguish between nominal and real GDP.
Nominal: at current prices. Real: adjusted for prices, shows actual growth.
What does the wage share tell you?

It shows what share of national income goes to employees, i.e. wages and salaries including employers' social contributions. The rest is the profit share (income from business and property). The wage share is a measure of income distribution, for example in collective bargaining. Formula to remember: employee compensation / national income × 100.
Why is GDP controversial as a measure of prosperity?
Unpaid work and the shadow economy are missing, environmental damage and accidents increase it, distribution and quality of life are left open.
Describe the four phases of the business cycle.
Upswing (expansion), boom, downturn (recession), trough (depression).
Distinguish between leading, coincident and lagging indicators and give one example of each.
Leading: incoming orders, business climate index, building permits. Coincident: GDP, production, capacity utilisation. Lagging: unemployment rate, prices, wages.
Explain anticyclical fiscal policy.
The state counteracts the cycle: in a downturn spend more and cut taxes, in a boom save and raise taxes.
Name the main goal and the instruments of the ECB.
Price stability (2 % in the medium term). Open market operations, standing facilities (marginal lending, deposit), minimum reserves.
Distinguish between expansionary and contractionary monetary policy.
Expansionary: lower interest rates and minimum reserves, buy securities, money supply rises. Contractionary: the opposite, to slow inflation.
Distinguish between inflation and deflation.
Inflation: persistently rising price level, purchasing power falls. Deflation: persistently falling price level, purchases are postponed, the economy shrinks.
What is the shopping basket?
Selection of typical goods and services of a household. Its price development gives the consumer price index.
Describe the structure of the balance of payments.
Current account (trade, services, primary and secondary income), capital account, financial account.
What are net exports?
Exports minus imports of goods and services. Positive net exports increase GDP and support employment.
Explain the term authorised dealer.
An independent dealer who sells new vehicles in their own name and for their own account.
Distinguish between direct and indirect sales.
Direct: the manufacturer sells itself (branch, online, agency). Indirect: via independent dealers.
Name features of the genuine agency model.
Sale in the name and for the account of the manufacturer, the manufacturer sets the price and bears stock and sales risk, the dealership receives commission.
Name advantages of the agency model for the dealership.
No capital tied up in vehicle stock, no sales or residual value risk, no discount competition, predictable commission.
Describe the multi-level distribution system.
The manufacturer delivers to an importer or main dealer, who delivers to sub-dealers, who then sell to the customer.
State who represents the interests of dealerships.
The ZDK (Central Association of the German Motor Trade) and the brand dealer associations.
Explain the term re-import.
A vehicle produced for another EU market that is imported into Germany. Usually cheaper, equipment may differ.
Name one advantage and one disadvantage of a pre-registration for the dealership.
Advantage: reach registration targets and bonuses. Disadvantage: sale at a high discount, costs of registration.
Name the components of the dealer margin.
Base margin (base discount), performance-related margin and bonuses (volume, customer satisfaction CSI, corporate design, standards).
Distinguish between gross profit and gross surplus on new cars.
Gross profit = margin − revenue reductions (discount, extras, overpayment on trade-in). Gross surplus = gross profit − salesperson commission.
Name the documents the customer receives at vehicle handover.
Registration certificate part I (and II), CoC, owner's manual, service book, warranty documents, invoice, handover record.
Name the documents needed for registration.
ID, eVB number (insurance confirmation), registration certificate II, CoC, SEPA mandate for vehicle tax. Companies also trade registration or commercial register extract.
Name sources of used cars.
Trade-ins, lease returns, free purchase, dealer colleagues, auctions, company and rental cars, online marketplaces.
Name examples of holding costs.
Interest on tied-up capital, loss in value, space costs, care and reconditioning, insurance.
Name causes of excessively long holding times.
Price too high, stock not in line with the market, poor reconditioning or presentation, weak ads, technical defects.
Explain what determines the capital requirement in the used car business.

Every used car ties up money from purchase until the customer has paid. So the capital requirement rises with the number of vehicles, their purchase price and every day in stock and of payment term. Shorter days in stock reduce it directly. Formula to remember: units per year × Ø purchase price × (days in stock + days until payment) / 360.
Name advantages of buying a used car from a dealership compared with a private sale.
Liability for defects, inspected vehicle, warranty, financing, trade-in, service.
Describe how a new car purchase contract is concluded.

The binding order is the offer. The contract is formed by an acceptance in text form (e.g. e-mail) or delivery within the binding period: 3 weeks (commercial vehicles 6 weeks), for vehicles available at the seller 10 days (commercial vehicles 2 weeks).
State when the purchase price is due.
On handover of the vehicle and delivery of the invoice.
Distinguish between a binding and a non-binding delivery date.
Binding: default immediately when exceeded. Non-binding: the buyer can demand delivery 6 weeks later, then default.
Explain the link between retention of title and registration certificate part II.
The vehicle remains the seller's property until full payment. Until then, the seller may keep registration certificate part II.
Distinguish between liability for defects and a guarantee.
Liability for defects: statutory, seller, defect at handover, 2 years. Guarantee: voluntary, manufacturer or guarantor, function during the term.
Describe the three options at the end of a three-way financing.
Pay the final instalment, refinance the final instalment or return the vehicle.
Describe the calculation scheme of a vehicle financing.

First you work out how much the customer really has to finance: price minus down payment and trade-in. Insurance financed along with it and the interest increase the loan. A final instalment is only paid at the end, so only the rest is spread over the monthly instalments. Scheme to remember: price − down payment − trade-in = remaining amount + insurance = net loan + interest = total loan − final instalment = sum of instalments / term = monthly instalment.
Name securities in car financing.
Transfer of ownership by way of security (registration certificate II at the bank), salary assignment, guarantee, payment protection insurance, comprehensive cover, down payment.
Name the key contents of the SECCI form.
Lender, type of credit, net loan amount, term, borrowing rate, effective annual rate, total amount, instalments, securities, right of withdrawal, early repayment.
Name negative entries at SCHUFA.
Terminated loan, payment order or enforcement, statement of assets, personal insolvency.
Describe what applies to cash payments from 10.000 €.
Money Laundering Act: identify the customer, document the transaction, report if suspicious.
Explain who owns the vehicle in leasing and who puts it on the balance sheet.
The lessor is the owner and capitalises it. The lessee is the possessor and books the instalments as an expense.
Distinguish between mileage and residual value leasing.
Mileage lease: settlement by kilometres driven, residual value risk with the lessor. Residual value lease: the lessee bears the residual value risk.
Name the insurances that are compulsory in leasing.
Motor third-party liability and comprehensive cover.
Describe which damage motor third-party liability covers.
Personal injury, property damage and financial loss caused to third parties.
Name the damage covered by partial cover (Teilkasko).
Fire, explosion, theft, storm, hail, lightning, flood, glass breakage, collision with game, marten bites, short circuit.
Name the damage comprehensive cover (Vollkasko) covers in addition.
Self-inflicted accident damage to your own vehicle and vandalism.
Explain why there are no no-claims classes in partial cover.
The insured damage does not depend on the insured person's driving behaviour.
Explain an economic total loss.
The repair costs exceed the replacement cost (replacement value minus residual value). The payout is replacement value minus residual value; with comprehensive cover also minus the deductible.
Explain what GAP insurance covers.
In the event of total loss or theft, it covers the gap between the replacement value and the outstanding balance or lease settlement.
Name advantages of warranty insurance for the dealership.
Customer loyalty, workshop utilisation, commission, sales argument, lower goodwill costs.
Explain when an expenditure is not (yet) an expense.
When the consumption of value only occurs later: purchase of goods for stock or of a fixed asset. The expense only arises on sale/use or through depreciation.
Explain imputed interest and why it is charged.

Equity could also earn interest elsewhere. Cost accounting counts this lost income as a cost, so that prices also cover interest on the company's own money. That is why interest is charged on all operationally necessary capital, not just on loans. Formula to remember: operationally necessary capital × imputed interest rate.
Name examples of imputed risks.
Bad debts, warranty and goodwill, shrinkage and theft in stores, loss in value of used cars. General entrepreneurial risk is not included; it is covered by profit.
Explain fixed cost degression.
As quantity increases, fixed costs are spread over more units. Fixed unit costs and thus total unit costs fall.
Describe how fixed and variable costs look in a diagram.

Total fixed costs: horizontal line. Total variable costs: rising straight line from the origin. Total costs: rising line starting at fixed costs. Where the revenue line intersects it is the break-even point.
Assess whether a product making a loss on a full-cost basis should be dropped.
Only if its contribution margin is negative. With a positive contribution margin it helps cover fixed costs. If it were dropped, the operating result would be worse.
Distinguish between time, company and industry comparison.
Time comparison: own figures from different periods. Company comparison: with other businesses. Industry comparison: with the industry average.
Explain what the debt ratio and fixed asset coverage II tell you.

The debt ratio shows how much debt there is in relation to equity: the higher it is, the more dependent on creditors and the riskier. Fixed asset coverage II checks the golden balance sheet rule: assets tied up long term, such as buildings and machines, should be financed with long-term capital, i.e. equity and long-term debt. It should be at least 100 %. Formula to remember: debt / equity × 100; (equity + long-term debt) / fixed assets × 100.
Explain what gross profit in percent tells you.

It shows what percentage of revenue remains after cost of goods to cover the other costs (staff, premises, administration) and make a profit. Falling gross profit is a warning sign, for example of discounts that are too high. Formula to remember: gross profit / net revenue × 100.
What does demand depend on?
Price of the good, income, prices of other goods (substitutes and complements), needs and fashion, expectations.
What does supply depend on?
Price of the good, cost of production factors, state of technology, profit expectations, number of suppliers, state levies and subsidies.
Distinguish between substitute and complementary goods.

Substitutes replace each other (butter and margarine): if one gets more expensive, demand for the other rises. Complements go together (car and fuel): if one gets more expensive, demand for the other falls too.
How does a subsidy to suppliers affect the market?
Suppliers' costs fall, supply rises (curve shifts right). The price falls, quantity rises. The price still forms freely: market-conforming.
Who makes economic policy?
Federal government, states and municipalities, the EU, the ECB and the Bundesbank, and the collective bargaining parties.
Name a goal conflict and a goal harmony.
Conflict: high employment and price stability; growth and environmental protection. Harmony: economic growth and high employment.
Describe GDP by production, expenditure and distribution.
Production: value added by economic sectors. Expenditure: consumption, investment, net exports. Distribution: employee compensation and business and property income.
Distinguish between primary and secondary income distribution.
Primary: the distribution the market produces (wage share, profit share). Secondary: distribution after state redistribution through taxes, social contributions and transfers.
Distinguish between cyclical and seasonal fluctuations.
Cyclical: medium term over several years, affect the whole economy. Seasonal: short term and due to the time of year, e.g. construction in winter, Christmas business.
Name examples of state revenue and spending policy.
Revenue: change tax rates, extend or reduce depreciation options. Spending: public contracts, investment programmes, subsidies, transfer payments.
What is the key interest rate and what does a cut do?
The rate at which banks borrow money from the ECB. Cut: loans get cheaper, investment and consumption rise, the economy is stimulated, the risk of inflation rises.
Name tasks of the Deutsche Bundesbank.
Implement ECB monetary policy in Germany, supply cash, process payments, take part in banking supervision, manage currency reserves.
Distinguish between the face value and the purchasing power of money.
Face value: the printed amount. Purchasing power: the amount of goods you can buy with it. With inflation, the face value stays the same, purchasing power falls.
Name opportunities and risks of globalisation.
Opportunities: larger sales markets, cheaper purchasing, more choice, division of labour. Risks: relocation of jobs, wage and price pressure, dependence on supply chains.
Name types of cartels.
Price cartel (uniform prices), territorial cartel (division of sales areas), quota cartel (quantities), bid-rigging cartel (agreements in tenders).
Explain what the Vertical Block Exemption Regulation (Vertikal-GVO) governs.

An EU regulation that exempts agreements between manufacturer and dealer (vertical) from the cartel ban under certain conditions. It thus allows selective and exclusive distribution systems in car retail.
Distinguish between a selective and an exclusive distribution system.

Selective: the manufacturer chooses dealers according to fixed criteria (standards, number); sales only to end customers and approved dealers. Exclusive: the dealer is assigned an area alone (territorial protection).
Name the partners in a manufacturer's sales network.
Manufacturer or importer, branches, authorised dealers (A and B dealers), agents, service partners (authorised workshops).
Explain the term service partner.
A workshop authorised by the manufacturer that offers maintenance, repair, warranty work and original parts but does not sell new cars in its own name (at most brokers them).
Name key contents of a dealer contract.
Contract territory, sales targets and minimum purchase, standards (equipment, corporate design, training), margin and bonus system, stock and demo car obligations, term and termination.
Distinguish between the training profile, the framework training plan and the framework curriculum.
Profile: skills and knowledge to be taught. Framework training plan: content and time structure for the company. Framework curriculum: vocational school content (learning fields).
Name duties of the apprentice and of the training company.

Apprentice: duty to learn, attend vocational school, follow instructions, keep a training record, confidentiality. Training company: train, provide training materials free of charge, release for vocational school, pay remuneration, issue a reference.
Who do you turn to with problems during training?
Trainer, youth representation (JAV) or works council, the IHK training adviser, the vocational school; in a dispute, the chamber's arbitration committee.
What does a works agreement govern?
A written agreement between employer and works council for all employees, e.g. working hours, flexitime, leave principles, breaks, monitoring.
Distinguish between active and passive voting rights.
Active: being allowed to vote. Passive: being eligible for election.
Name rights of the works council.
Right to information, consultation and hearing (e.g. before dismissals), participation in personnel measures (hiring, transfer), co-determination in social matters.
Distinguish between need, requirement and demand.
Need: feeling of lack. Requirement: need backed by purchasing power. Demand: requirement actually expressed on the market.
Describe the three economic sectors.
Primary: raw production (raw materials, agriculture). Secondary: processing (carmakers, suppliers). Tertiary: services (dealership, bank, insurance).
Name types of goods.
Physical goods, services, rights. Consumer and capital goods. Durable and consumable goods.
Assign legal forms to partnerships and corporations.
Partnerships: OHG, KG, GmbH & Co. KG. Corporations: GmbH, AG. The e. K. is a sole proprietorship.
What is a GmbH & Co. KG?
A KG whose fully liable partner (Komplementär) is a GmbH. This effectively limits liability to the GmbH's assets and the limited partners' contributions.
Describe the profit distribution in a KG.
According to the partnership agreement; without a provision, since 2024 according to the agreed shareholdings. Limited partners share in losses only up to their contribution.
What is the commercial register?
A public register of merchants kept at the local court. Section A: sole traders and partnerships. Section B: corporations.
Distinguish between the declaratory and the constitutive effect of an entry.

Declaratory: the fact applies before, registration makes it known, e.g. „Istkaufmann“ (merchant by nature of business), „Prokura“. Constitutive: only registration creates the right, e.g. GmbH, AG, „Kannkaufmann“ (optional merchant).
„Ist-“, „Kann-“ and „Formkaufmann“?

„Istkaufmann“: runs a commercial business that requires commercial organisation. „Kannkaufmann“: small business or agriculture/forestry, registered voluntarily. „Formkaufmann“: by virtue of legal form, e.g. GmbH, AG.
What is the „Firma“?
The name under which a merchant does business, signs, sues and can be sued.
Name the types of „Handlungsvollmacht“.
General (all ordinary business), specific type (a certain type of business, e.g. purchasing), single (one single transaction); each also possible as joint authority with others.
Distinguish between legal subjects and legal objects.
Legal subjects: bearers of rights and obligations (natural and legal persons). Legal objects: items of legal transactions (things and rights).
Name examples of legal persons under private and public law.
Private: GmbH, AG, registered association. Public: federal government, states, municipalities, IHK, pension insurance.
Distinguish between an enquiry, an offer and an advertisement.
Enquiry: non-binding. Offer: binding declaration of intent to a specific person. Advertisement (brochure, shop window, online shop): aimed at the general public, not an offer.
How long is an offer binding?

Between people present and on the phone: only immediately. Between absent parties: as long as an answer usually takes (letter about a week, e-mail one to two days). Offer with a deadline: until the deadline.
What do exclusion clauses do?
They restrict or remove the binding nature of the offer: „subject to change“, „non-binding“, „while stocks last“, „price subject to change“.
How is a purchase contract concluded?
Through offer and acceptance: offer + order, or order without offer + order confirmation or delivery.
Distinguish between the obligation and the fulfilment transaction.
Obligation: concluding the contract. Fulfilment: the seller delivers free of defects and transfers ownership; the buyer accepts and pays.
What form requirements exist?

Written form (handwritten signature, e.g. dismissal, guarantee), public certification (signature confirmed, e.g. commercial register application), notarial certification (content and signature, e.g. property purchase).
Explain freedom of contract and its limits.
Freedom to conclude, determine content and form. Limits: laws, good morals, form requirements, obligation to contract (e.g. motor liability), AGB law.
Name the types of material defects.
Defect in quality, wrong delivery, short delivery, installation defect, faulty installation instructions, deviation from advertising claims.
Distinguish between defects by how recognisable they are.
Obvious defect (visible immediately), hidden defect (only appears later), fraudulently concealed defect (seller knew; limitation 3 years).
Name the secondary rights for material defects and their requirement.

Withdrawal (not for a minor defect), price reduction, damages instead of performance (if at fault), reimbursement of wasted expenses. Requirement: supplementary performance has failed (deadline passed, two failed attempts) or was refused.
Distinguish between a consumer sale, a civil sale and one-sided and two-sided commercial sales.

Consumer sale: a business sells goods to a consumer. One-sided commercial sale: only one party is a merchant (e.g. a dealership sells to or buys from a private customer). Civil sale: private to private. Two-sided commercial sale: merchant to merchant.
Describe the buyer's rights in case of late delivery.
Without grace period: demand delivery and compensation for damage caused by delay. After an unsuccessful grace period: withdrawal and/or damages instead of performance.
Distinguish between concrete and abstract damage.
Concrete: exactly provable, e.g. extra price of a cover purchase. Abstract: only estimable, e.g. lost profit.
Distinguish between quantitative and qualitative comparison of offers.
Quantitative: compare landed costs (list price − discount − cash discount + delivery costs). Qualitative: weight and score other criteria (scoring: quality, delivery time, reliability, service).
What is the optimal order quantity?
The quantity at which the sum of ordering and storage costs is lowest. Large quantities: low ordering, high storage costs; small quantities the reverse.
Explain minimum, reorder and maximum stock.

Minimum stock is the safety reserve for delivery delays and is normally not touched. The reorder point is set so that stock lasts until the next delivery. When it is reached, an order is placed. Maximum stock is the upper limit, so that not too much capital and space is tied up. Formula to remember: reorder point = daily usage × delivery time + minimum stock; maximum stock = minimum stock + order quantity.
Distinguish between the reorder point and the fixed-interval ordering method.
Reorder point: order when the reorder level is reached. Fixed interval: order at fixed time intervals.
Name the functions of a warehouse.
Security (availability), bridging (time between purchase and sale), speculation (buy cheaply), transformation (sort, portion), refinement (ripening).
Name types of storage costs.
Space costs (rent, energy, depreciation), personnel costs, inventory costs (capital tied up/interest, shrinkage, insurance).
Describe the procedure for incoming goods inspection.

Immediately in the driver's presence: address, number and condition of packages. Then without delay: compare delivery note with order, check type, quantity and quality, report defects, store and book goods.
Distinguish between the fixed and the free location system.
Fixed location: each item has its fixed place (clear, needs more space). Free location (chaotic): the IT system assigns the next free place (space-saving, nothing can be found without IT).
Distinguish between FiFo and LiFo.
First in, first out: what was stored first goes out first (important for ageing). Last in, first out: what was stored last goes out first.
Explain the just-in-time method with one advantage and one disadvantage.
Goods are delivered exactly when needed. Hardly any storage costs, but dependence on the supplier and transport routes.
Distinguish between a direct debit and a standing order.
Direct debit: the recipient collects, amount and date can vary (SEPA mandate). Standing order: the payer instructs their bank to pay a fixed amount on fixed dates.
Is cash discount worth it with a loan?

Not taking the discount really means taking a loan from the supplier, for the days between the discount period and the payment term. This supplier credit is very expensive: 2 % discount at 10 instead of 30 days equals about 36 % interest per year. That is why it is almost always worth taking a cheaper bank loan and paying with the discount. Formula to remember: annual rate ≈ discount rate × 360 / (payment term − discount period).
Distinguish between range width and range depth.
Width: number of product groups (wide or narrow). Depth: choice within a product group (deep or shallow). More variants of an existing item make the range deeper.
Distinguish between the core and the peripheral range.
Core range: items that bring the main revenue and belong to the business purpose (e.g. wiper blades). Peripheral range: supplementary items (e.g. mug with logo).
Name the phases of a sales conversation.
Greeting, needs analysis, product demonstration, sales arguments, closing the sale, farewell.
What types of questions are there?
Open question (W question), closed question (yes/no), alternative question (this or that), leading question (suggests the answer), rhetorical question (you answer it yourself).
Describe the customer-oriented chain of arguments.
Name the product feature, describe the product advantage, derive the customer benefit.
Distinguish between verbal and non-verbal communication.
Verbal: the spoken word. Non-verbal: body language such as facial expression, gestures, posture, eye contact, clothing.
Name the four shelf zones.
Stretch zone (overhead), eye level zone (best-selling zone), grab zone (hip to chest height), bend zone (bottom).
What is an add-on sale?
A suitable additional item is specifically recommended with the main item, with a concrete benefit for the customer.
Distinguish between a liability case and a comprehensive cover case.
Liability damage: someone else caused the damage, their insurance pays. Comprehensive damage: your own comprehensive cover pays the damage to your own vehicle.
Name claims of the injured party in a liability case.
Repair costs or replacement cost, expert fees, reduction in market value, rental car or loss of use, towing costs, flat-rate expenses, lawyer's fees.
Describe the claims in a comprehensive cover case.
Only the contractual benefit: repair costs or replacement value minus residual value and deductible. Usually no reduction in value and no loss of use.
What is the repair cost assumption (RKÜ) with assignment by way of security?

The customer assigns their claim against the insurer to the dealership. The dealership invoices the insurer directly and thus secures payment. If the insurer doesn't pay, the customer remains the debtor.
What applies if the customer is entitled to deduct input VAT?
The insurer only reimburses the net amount. The customer pays the VAT to the dealership and reclaims it as input VAT from the tax office.
Distinguish between a technical and an economic total loss.

Technical: repair is no longer possible. Economic: the repair costs exceed the replacement cost (replacement value minus residual value). For liability claims, repair may still be allowed under the 130 % rule if its conditions are met.
What does the 130 % rule say?
In a liability case, the repair may cost up to 130 % of the replacement value if the car is fully and professionally repaired and kept in use (usually at least 6 months).
What is the integrity interest?
The injured party's interest in keeping their familiar vehicle. It justifies the 130 % rule.
Explain the reduction in market value (merkantile Wertminderung).
The loss in value that remains despite professional repair, because the vehicle fetches less on the market as an accident car.
Explain loss of use (Nutzungsausfall).
Daily compensation for the injured party in a liability case who does without a rental car. Requirement: will and ability to use the car.
Explain strict liability (Gefährdungshaftung).
The keeper is liable for the operating risk of their vehicle even without own fault. That's why motor liability insurance is compulsory.
Who commissions the expert?
In a liability case the injured party (above the minor damage limit); the other side's insurer pays. In a comprehensive cover case the insurer decides.
What counts as game (Haarwild) under partial cover?
For example deer, stag, wild boar, hare, wild rabbit, fox, badger, marten. Birds and pets are not included unless the policy covers „animals of all kinds“.
Name advantages and disadvantages of a workshop commitment clause.
Pro: lower comprehensive premium, often pick-up and delivery. Con: the insurer chooses the workshop; with leasing, financing or a manufacturer warranty this can cause problems.
Why is full-service accident handling important for the dealership?
The customer gets everything from one source (expert, rental car, repair, settlement). That retains them, keeps the workshop and paint shop busy and brings parts and rental revenue.
Name risks of a notional settlement based on the expert report.
Only the net amount without VAT is paid; insurers often cut hourly rates; hidden damage goes undetected; the dealership loses the repair order.
Describe how to determine the purchase price of a used car.
Backwards from the achievable selling price: convert to net, then deduct gross profit (profit and costs), repairs, reconditioning, warranty and holding costs.
Name factors that affect the purchase price.
Age, mileage, condition, accident-free, equipment, colour, number of previous owners, service book, MOT (HU), market situation and season.
State who values the used car at the dealership.
Technical valuation: workshop or used car master (condition, repair costs). Commercial valuation: used car sales manager with DAT or Schwacke and market observation.
Explain the meaning of „VAT deductible“ (Mehrwertsteuer ausweisbar).
The vehicle is standard-taxed; the invoice shows 19 % VAT. Interesting for business customers who can deduct input VAT.
Explain why margin taxation exists.
To avoid double taxation: the purchase price from a private seller already contains VAT that the dealer cannot deduct as input VAT.
Explain a hidden price discount and who bears it.
The trade-in is credited above its actual value in order to sell the new car. The overpayment is borne by the new car department; the used car is booked at its real value.
Name reasons why a calculated used car price is often not achieved.
Long holding time, falling market prices, model change, undetected defects, season, strong competing offers.
Name reasons for actively buying in used cars.
Fill gaps in the range, offer models in demand, meet demand, keep sales and workshop busy, additional profit.
Distinguish between capacity to borrow and creditworthiness.
Capacity: legally able to conclude loan contracts (full legal capacity). Creditworthiness: personal and economic circumstances make repayment likely.
Name documents used to check creditworthiness.
Private person: proof of salary, self-disclosure, SCHUFA report, ID. Company: balance sheet and P&L, business analysis, commercial register extract, credit agency.
Explain the identity check (Legitimationsprüfung).
Establishing the customer's identity using ID card or passport (for companies also the commercial register extract). Required under the Money Laundering Act.
Distinguish between a deficiency guarantee and an absolute guarantee.
Deficiency: the guarantor only pays after unsuccessful enforcement against the debtor. Absolute (selbstschuldnerisch): the bank can turn to the guarantor immediately (usual bank form).
Explain what the effective annual rate tells you.
The total cost of credit per year in percent including fees. Only with it can offers be compared.
Explain an annuity loan.
A loan with a constant instalment. The interest portion falls with the outstanding balance, the repayment portion rises.
Name ways of lowering the monthly instalment.
Higher down payment, longer term, higher final instalment, lower interest, cheaper vehicle or less equipment.
Explain the term linked transaction.
Purchase contract and loan form an economic unit. If the customer withdraws from the loan (14 days), the purchase contract also lapses.
Explain why there is often no discount for cash buyers.
The dealership receives commission for brokered financing and leasing and retains the customer until the end of the contract. Cash payment brings it no advantage.
Distinguish between two-way and three-way financing.
Two ways: pay the final instalment or refinance. Three ways: additionally return the vehicle to the dealer.
Name three differences between leasing and renting.
Leasing has a fixed, longer term without ordinary termination; the lessee bears maintenance, insurance and the risk of loss and damage; the vehicle is purchased for them.
Explain tax-compliant leasing (erlasskonform).
The basic lease term is between 40 % and 90 % of the normal useful life. Then the vehicle is attributed to the lessor for tax purposes and the instalments are operating expenses for the lessee.
Explain the tender right (Andienungsrecht).
The lessor can oblige the lessee to buy the vehicle at the agreed residual value at the end of the contract. The lessee has no right to buy.
Distinguish between full and partial amortisation.
Full: the instalments fully cover acquisition cost, interest and the lessor's profit. Partial: a residual value remains open, which must be covered at the end.
Explain the role of VAT in leasing.
It is due on each instalment and the special payment, not all at once on the purchase price. That protects liquidity; businesses deduct it as input VAT.
Explain why dealerships offer almost only mileage leasing.
The customer has no residual value risk and clear costs. Only extra and fewer kilometres and damage beyond normal wear are settled.
Name the contents of the return record.
Mileage, damage outside and inside, tyre condition, completeness of accessories, keys and papers, service book, signatures.
Name the services included in full-service leasing.
Besides use, also maintenance and wear repairs, tyres, often insurance, tax and a replacement car. Advantage: fixed, predictable monthly costs.
Describe the term and cancellation of motor insurance.
One year, usually until 31 Dec, cancellation by 30 Nov. Special cancellation after a premium increase, after a claim and when changing vehicles.
Name ways of lowering the motor insurance premium.
High no-claims class, favourable type and regional class, low mileage, garage, restricted drivers, deductible, workshop commitment.
Explain no-claims protection (Rabattschutz).
For an extra premium, the no-claims class is kept after one claim per year.
Explain the meaning of the security certificate (Sicherungsschein).
In a claim, the comprehensive payout goes to the lessor or bank because they own the vehicle or it was transferred to them as security.
Distinguish between a guarantee, statutory warranty and goodwill.
Statutory warranty (liability for defects): the seller's legal duty. Guarantee: voluntary promise. Goodwill: voluntary accommodation without legal claim, usually after deadlines have passed.
Distinguish between quantitative and qualitative staffing requirements.
Quantitative: how many employees are needed. Qualitative: which qualifications they must have.
Name advantages and disadvantages of internal and external recruitment.

Internal: fast, cheap, motivating, applicant known; but tunnel vision, the old position becomes vacant, envy. External: large choice, new ideas; but more expensive, longer onboarding, risk of a wrong hire.
Describe the recruitment process.
Determine need, job description and posting, screen applications, interviews, selection with works council involvement, employment contract, onboarding.
Name key contents of an employment contract.
Parties, start (and fixed term), place of work, job, pay, working hours, leave, probation, notice periods, reference to collective agreement and works agreements.
Name rights and duties of the employee.
Rights: pay, leave, welfare, reference, continued pay when sick. Duties: work performance, follow instructions, confidentiality, loyalty and non-competition.
Distinguish between a simple and a qualified job reference.
Simple: type and duration of work. Qualified: also performance and conduct. It must be true and benevolent; errors can be corrected on request, if necessary at the labour court.
Name key rules of the Working Hours Act.
8 hours per working day, up to 10 hours with compensation; break 30 minutes for more than 6 hours, 45 minutes for more than 9 hours; 11 hours rest.
State the protection periods under the Maternity Protection Act.
Protection period 6 weeks before and 8 weeks after birth (12 weeks for premature and multiple births). Ban on dismissal from the start of pregnancy until 4 months after delivery.
Explain how the taxable benefit of a company car is determined using the 1 % method.

Round the gross list price down to full 100 €. Combustion engine: 1 % of it per month plus 0.03 % per km of distance to work. Pure electric cars: a quarter, plug-in hybrids: half of these values (under conditions). The amount increases taxable and social security gross pay and is deducted again from net pay.
Describe who receives which payment from the payslip.

Employee: payout amount. Tax office: income tax, solidarity surcharge, church tax. Health insurance fund: all social security contributions (collection agency). Bank or building society: capital-forming benefits.
Name the components of the employer's personnel costs.
Gross pay + employer social security shares + accident insurance contribution + voluntary benefits.
Distinguish between ordinary dismissal, extraordinary dismissal and a termination agreement.
Ordinary: with notice. Extraordinary: without notice for good cause, within 2 weeks of knowledge. Termination agreement: by mutual consent, without notice, in writing.
Distinguish between personal, conduct-related and operational dismissal.
Personal: reason lies in the person (long illness, loss of driving licence). Conduct-related: breach of duty, warning first. Operational: job is cut, social selection necessary.
Name the criteria for social selection.
Length of service, age, maintenance obligations, severe disability.
Explain the function of a formal warning (Abmahnung).
It criticises specific misconduct, demands change and threatens dismissal if repeated. In writing as proof.
State the notice period an employee must give.

With the basic period of 4 weeks to the 15th or end of month, 2 weeks during probation, unless the contract or collective agreement says otherwise. The longer periods based on length of service only apply to the employer by law. By contract, the employee's period may not be longer than the employer's.
Describe the role of the works council in dismissals.

It must be consulted before every dismissal, otherwise it is invalid. For an ordinary dismissal it can raise concerns or object within one week; for a dismissal without notice it can only raise concerns within 3 days.
Distinguish between a framework and a pay agreement.

Framework agreement: long-term working conditions (hours, leave, notice periods, bonuses). Pay agreement: amount of wages and training pay, short term because adjusted regularly to prices and the economy.
What does general applicability mean?
The Ministry of Labour declares a collective agreement valid for all employers and employees in the industry, including those not bound by it.
Distinguish between a strike, a lockout and arbitration.
Strike: employees stop work. Lockout: employers refuse work and pay. Arbitration: a neutral arbitrator proposes a settlement.
Which risks does social insurance not cover and what helps?

Occupational disability, liability for damage to others, accidents in leisure time, pension gap in old age. Remedy: disability, private liability and private accident insurance, private pension provision.
Name forms of private pension provision and how they are supported.
Riester pension (allowances and special expense deduction), occupational pension (tax and contribution-free salary conversion), basic pension/Rürup (special expense deduction).
Name the seven types of income.
Agriculture and forestry, trade or business, self-employment, employment, capital assets, renting and leasing, other income.
How do you calculate taxable income?
Income − income-related expenses (at least the 1.230 € allowance) = earnings − special expenses − extraordinary burdens = taxable income. Refund = income tax withheld − tax assessed.
Distinguish between stocktaking (Inventur) and the inventory list (Inventar).
Stocktaking: the activity, i.e. counting, measuring, weighing and valuing all assets and debts. Inventory list: the result, a detailed list by type, quantity and value.
Distinguish between physical and book stocktaking.
Physical: stock is actually counted, measured or weighed (vehicles, parts). Book: intangible values are determined from documents and books (receivables, bank balances, debts).
Name the stocktaking methods.
Cut-off date: within 10 days around the balance sheet date. Shifted: up to 3 months before or 2 months after, rolled forward or back. Perpetual: ongoing stock records, each item counted once a year.
State when stocktaking is required.
On founding or takeover, at the end of each financial year and on dissolution or sale of the company.
Explain the lower of cost or market principle.

Of acquisition cost and current value on the reporting date, the lower one is used. Example: a part bought for 100 € is only worth 80 €, so 80 € is recognised. This applies strictly to current assets; for fixed assets only if the loss in value is permanent. Unrealised gains may not be shown.
Describe the structure of the inventory list.
A assets: fixed assets, then current assets, ordered by increasing liquidity. B debts: long-term, then short-term, ordered by due date. C net worth (equity) = assets − debts.
Explain the link between stocktaking, the inventory list and the balance sheet.
Stocktaking provides the data, the inventory list lists them in detail, the balance sheet summarises them briefly in account form: assets and liabilities/equity.
Describe the structure of the balance sheet and explain why both sides are equal.
Assets: fixed assets, current assets (use of funds). Liabilities: equity, debt (source of funds). Both sides show the same capital from two angles; equity balances as the residual.
Describe the four balance sheet changes with one example each.

Asset exchange: only asset accounts, total stays (cash withdrawal). Liability exchange: only liability accounts, total stays (payable becomes loan). Increase on both sides (purchase on credit). Decrease on both sides (invoice paid by bank).
Explain what the debt ratio tells you.

It shows what share of total capital comes from creditors, for example banks and suppliers. The higher it is, the more dependent the company is and the more interest and repayments it has to make. Equity and debt ratio together make 100 %. Formula to remember: debt / total capital × 100.
Describe how bookings are made on asset and liability accounts.

Asset account: opening balance and increases on the debit side, decreases and closing balance on the credit side. Liability account exactly the reverse: opening balance and increases on the credit side.
Distinguish between the journal and the general ledger.
Journal: all booking records in chronological order. General ledger: the same bookings sorted by account (T-accounts).
Distinguish between balance sheet accounts and income statement accounts.
Balance sheet accounts show assets and debts and are closed via the closing balance sheet account. Income statement accounts (expenses and income) change equity and are closed via the P&L account.
Distinguish between transactions that do not affect profit and those that do.
Not affecting profit: only balance sheet accounts are involved, equity stays the same (purchase on credit). Affecting profit: an expense or income account is involved, equity changes (rent, sale).
Explain why there is a VAK booking.
On sale, revenue is booked. The VAK booking sets the cost of goods at cost price against it as an expense and reduces stock. Only revenue minus VAK shows the gross profit.
Describe how income statement accounts flow into the closing.
Operating expenses and income give the operating result, neutral ones the neutral result. Both flow into the P&L account. Its balance (profit or loss) goes to equity.
Describe how to check a booking record.

Total debit = total credit; at least one account on the debit and one on the credit side; increase or decrease on the correct side; does the booking match the document? Order: debit first, then credit.
Name the VAT rates with examples.
Standard rate 19 %. Reduced rate 7 % for basic goods such as food, books, newspapers and local transport. Exempt are e.g. insurance, bank interest, residential rent, letter postage.
Explain why VAT is also called value added tax.
At each stage, only the value added is taxed, i.e. the difference between selling and purchase price. The basis is the net amount. It is borne by the end consumer.
Explain why VAT is a transitory item for the company.
It collects VAT from the customer, deducts the input VAT paid and only pays the difference to the tax office. It is neither expense nor income and doesn't change profit.
Explain input VAT, output VAT and VAT payable.

Input VAT: tax on incoming invoices, a receivable from the tax office. Output VAT: tax on outgoing invoices, a debt to the tax office. VAT payable = output VAT − input VAT. If input VAT is higher, there is an input VAT surplus (refund).
Describe how the tax accounts are closed.

The input VAT account is closed via the output VAT account (1770 Output VAT to 1570 Deductible input VAT). The VAT payable is transferred (1770 Output VAT to 1200 Bank), at year end carried into the closing balance sheet as a liability.
Explain the advance VAT return.
The regular report of VAT payable to the tax office, usually monthly or quarterly, electronically by the 10th day after the end of the period.
Explain what portfolio analysis shows.
It classifies models by market growth and relative market share: question marks (high growth, small share), stars (both high), cash cows (low growth, high share, bring money), poor dogs (both low).
Assign suitable strategies to the fields of the portfolio analysis.
Question marks: invest or give up. Stars: invest and expand. Cash cows: skim profits. Poor dogs: let them run out.
Distinguish between market potential, market volume and market share.
Market potential: maximum possible sales in the market. Market volume: actual sales of all suppliers. Market share: own sales as a percentage of market volume.
Describe how to plan next year's sales figure.
Expected market volume in the market area × target market share = planned sales. Compared with previous year's figures, new models and manufacturer targets.
Distinguish between the simple and the real capital requirement in the new car business.

New cars tie up money for as long as they stand at the dealer. In the simple view only these days in stock count. In reality more comes in: if the dealer gives the customer a payment term, the money is tied up longer. If the dealer pays the manufacturer later or the customer makes a down payment, it is tied up for less time. Formula to remember (simple): sales × cost price × days in stock / 360.
Describe the process of a new car order up to the order confirmation.

Needs analysis and advice, test drive, configuration and offer, binding customer order, credit and availability check, order with the manufacturer, order confirmation in text form within the binding period.
Name the components of a salesperson's pay.
Fixed salary, commission, bonuses (e.g. for financing, target achievement), often plus a company car as a taxable benefit.
Distinguish between revenue commission and gross profit commission.
Revenue commission: percentage of the net selling price; tempts to give high discounts. Gross profit commission: percentage of gross profit; the salesperson earns more by giving little discount.
Explain why a timely order confirmation in text form is important.
Only it accepts the customer's order and creates the purchase contract. If it comes after the binding period, the customer is no longer bound; it then counts as a new offer.
Name mandatory details on a new car outgoing invoice.
Name and address of dealership and customer, tax number or VAT ID, invoice number and date, delivery date, exact vehicle description with VIN, net amount, tax rate, tax amount, gross amount.
Explain why there is no VAT on registration fees.

The dealership pays the official fee to the authority in the name and for the account of the customer. It is a transitory item. The dealership's own registration service fee, however, is subject to VAT.
Explain the term internal order.

A workshop service for another department of the same company, e.g. pre-delivery inspection of a new car or reconditioning of a used car. It is charged internally without VAT and debited to the receiving department.
Describe how the purchase of a new car with delivery is booked.
3000 new car stock + 3030 delivery stock + 1570 input VAT to 1600 payables.
Explain when general terms and conditions may deviate from the law.

Only where the law is not mandatory and only without unreasonable disadvantage to the customer. For consumers, the protective rules (e.g. 2 years' liability for defects on new goods) cannot be waived; between merchants more is possible.
State the warranty periods for new and used cars.

New cars: 2 years. Used cars to consumers: can be shortened to 1 year if the customer is specifically informed beforehand and it is agreed expressly and separately (§ 476 (2) BGB). Used cars between businesses: can be excluded. Private to private: can be excluded, except for fraud.
Name ways of improving return on sales.
Cut costs or increase earnings per sale (better margins, more service and parts business). More revenue alone only helps if profit grows too.
Explain the „Kfz-Potenzial“ (vehicle potential) and how it is calculated.

The Kfz-Potenzial is the total stock of cars in the market area, regardless of brand. It shows how big the market for sales and service is overall. It is estimated from the number of inhabitants and the car density. Formula to remember: inhabitants / 1.000 × cars per 1.000 inhabitants. Example: 530.000 / 1.000 × 481 = 254.930 cars.
Describe how to get from the „Kfz-Potenzial“ to the annual demand for new cars.
Divide the „Kfz-Potenzial“ by the average useful life, because each vehicle is then replaced by a new car. Example: 254.930 / 5 = 50.986 new cars per year. For one month, divide by 12 again.
Describe how to calculate the previous year's value from a percentage change.

The percentage refers to the previous year's value, not to the current value. So the current value is, for example, 115 % of the previous year. That is why you do not simply subtract 15 %; you work back to 100 %. Formula to remember: current value / (1 + change / 100). Example: 230 cars at +15 % → 230 / 1,15 = 200 cars.
Describe the phases of a model's product life cycle.
Introduction, growth, maturity, saturation, decline. Sales rise slowly at first, then strongly, peak in the maturity phase and fall afterwards.
A model's sales already collapse in the growth phase. Name measures the manufacturer can take.
Check the causes (price, competition, quality, image) and counteract: model update or facelift, special editions, better equipment, price or financing offers, more advertising.
Describe how to calculate the planned figure for a quarter.
Annual plan × quarter share, usually rounded up to whole units. Example: 800 cars × 28 % = 224 cars in the 1st quarter.
Describe the contractual relationships between customer, dealership and bank in vehicle financing.

Customer and dealership: purchase contract (both sides), down payment to the dealership, handover of the vehicle to the customer. Customer and bank: loan agreement (both sides), instalments to the bank. Bank to dealership: payout of the loan.
Explain what the final instalment of three-way financing is based on.

The expected residual value (used car value) of the vehicle at the end of the term. It depends on model, equipment, term and mileage. That way the customer can return the car and the final instalment is covered.
Name data that SCHUFA stores.

Personal data (name, date of birth, addresses) as well as current accounts, credit cards, loans and instalment purchases (amount, term, repayment), leasing contracts, mobile phone and telecom contracts, guarantees and negative entries such as payment defaults.
Name reasons for which the bank can terminate a car loan.

Payment default: at least two consecutive instalments wholly or partly unpaid, plus 10 % (5 % for terms over 3 years) of the loan, and a 2-week deadline has passed without payment. Also: significant deterioration of financial circumstances, false information in the loan application, loss of the security (e.g. vehicle sold without consent, no comprehensive cover).
Name advantages that leasing contracts bring the dealership.

Commission from the leasing company, immediate payment for the vehicle without own default risk, customer loyalty and follow-up business after the contract ends, workshop utilisation during the term, a predictable supply of young used cars (lease returns), low instalments as a sales argument.
Describe how the leasing company calculates the result of a contract (final calculation).

Income: all lease payments (payment × term), extra kilometres (driven − agreed km − allowance, × rate) and the sale proceeds of the vehicle. Expenses: acquisition cost and costs before the sale (e.g. tyres, appraisal). Surplus = income − expenses. Fewer kilometres would reduce the income.
How is a purchase contract concluded?
Through two matching declarations of intent: offer and acceptance. Example: a binding offer from the supplier and a timely order.
Name the duties of seller and buyer under a contract of sale.
Seller: hand over the goods free of defects and transfer ownership. Buyer: accept the goods and pay the purchase price.
When is an offer binding and for how long?

An offer to a specific person is binding unless it contains exclusion clauses such as „freibleibend“ (subject to change). Between people present and by phone it only applies immediately, in writing for as long as a reply can normally be expected.
What must be observed at goods receipt between merchants?

Immediately: external check of packaging, number of packages and delivery address while the driver is present. Promptly: check the goods themselves (type, quantity, quality). Report defects promptly, otherwise the rights are lost (§ 377 HGB).
Distinguish between obvious, hidden and fraudulently concealed defects.

Obvious: recognisable immediately. Hidden: only appears later, report promptly after discovery. Fraudulently concealed: the seller knew about the defect and kept quiet. Longer limitation: 3 years from the end of the year in which the buyer learns of the defect, at most 10 years.
What does retention of title govern?
The goods remain the seller's property until paid in full. The buyer becomes the possessor on handover. If he does not pay, the seller can demand the goods back after withdrawing from the contract.
What belongs in a workshop order?
Customer and vehicle data (VIN, registration, mileage), the exact work, price range or cost estimate, completion date, test drive and old parts agreement, customer signature.
What is direct vehicle reception?
Receiving the vehicle together with the customer directly at the car, often on the lift. Defects become visible, the customer understands the order and extra work can be discussed straight away.
What are labour time units (AW)?
